I've farmed this land in Quzhou my whole life. My father farmed it, I farm it, and I know what grows here. The soil is sandy loam, the water table has been dropping for years, and my knees aren't what they were. I don't take risks with new crops. I plant wheat in autumn and follow it with maize in summer — that's what this land is for, that's what I know how to do, and that's what the grain station will buy.

I have about 9 mu of flat cropland. I'll keep it simple: all 9 mu in the wheat-maize rotation. I've been planting "矮抗58" wheat for years — good lodging resistance, the local seed shop always has it. For maize I use hybrid "郑单958," same as most people in the village. These aren't traditional seeds but they're what works here now.

For wheat I'll apply base fertilizer before planting — diammonium phosphate and urea together — then top-dress urea at jointing. Three irrigations: one before freeze-up, one at jointing, one at heading. I know I should maybe cut to two to save water, but I've seen what happens to yield when you skip the heading water. Three it is.

For maize after the wheat harvest, I won't plough — just rotary till lightly or go straight to planting to save time and moisture. Summer rains usually come, so I'll irrigate maybe once at tasseling if it's dry. One herbicide spray early, one for pests if I see borer damage.

I also keep a small vegetable patch behind the house — maybe half a mu — but that's for eating, not selling, so I won't count it in the plan.
